clue.text: Embrace troubles old Bob?

parts.note: cares are worries or troubles
a bob was the old shilling, abbreviated s

explanation.surface: Someone hugs an old friend called Bob to ease his troubles.
explanation.walkthrough: Bob looks like a man's name, but a bob was slang for a shilling, the pre-decimal British coin written s.
explanation.definitionFit: A caress is a gentle stroke or hug, so the noun matches a tender embrace.

clue.text: Name that is inspiring work?

parts.note: to call someone something is to name them

indicators.note: inspiring literally means breathing in, so one piece is drawn inside the other

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is
op, short for opus, is a musical work

explanation.surface: A riddle asking for the name of whatever spurs on creative work.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue describes a Muse, whose name is one that inspires work; 'inspiring' means breathing in as well as encouraging.
explanation.definitionFit: Calliope is the Muse of epic poetry, one of the goddesses believed to inspire poets.

clue.text: Game not available for extensive period: leave

parts.note: RU is rugby union
n/a is the abbreviation for not available
to last long is to go on for an extended time

explanation.surface: A match is off for a long time, so everyone should go home.
explanation.definitionFit: Run along is an idiom telling someone, often a child, to go away, so it means leave.

clue.text: Resentful about cocaine search

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word wraps around the other

parts.note: sour means bitter or resentful
C is slang shorthand for cocaine

explanation.surface: A bitter person is caught up in a drug search.
explanation.definitionFit: To scour an area is to search it thoroughly and rapidly, combing every part.

clue.text: Following vehicle note nasty woman's in state no more?

parts.note: a car is a road vehicle

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it, wrapped by the outer letters

parts.note: te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale
a hag is an unpleasant old woman

explanation.surface: A cryptic tale of a car chase and a nasty woman in some vanished country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' tells you the rest of the wordplay comes after the vehicle; 'state no more' points to a city-state that has vanished from the map.
explanation.definitionFit: Carthage was an ancient North African city-state destroyed by Rome, so it is a state that exists no longer.

clue.text: Reformed madam in career that shows anything is possible

indicators.note: reformed means made over in a new shape, so the letters are reorganised

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A former brothel keeper goes straight in a new career, proving anyone can make it.
explanation.walkthrough: Madam suggests a brothel keeper turning respectable, a neat illustration of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The American dream is the ideal that through hard work anybody in the US can succeed.

clue.text: Bombast, that — unctuous at first, unusually rigid, extremely tacky

indicators.note: at first points to the start, here of both preceding words

parts.note: the first letter of that

indicators.note: unusually means not in the normal way, so the letters take an odd order
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only those letters stay

parts.note: the first letter of unctuous
taken as written
the outside letters of tacky

explanation.surface: A list of faults in pompous speech: oily, stiff and tasteless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That' looks like a pointer back to Bombast, but 'at first' applies to it as well as to unctuous.
explanation.definitionFit: Turgidity, in writing or speech, means swollen pompous language, the same as bombast.

clue.text: Vamp at heart said to be without principles

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, so only the middle letters are kept

parts.note: the middle two letters of vamp
oral means spoken, said rather than written

explanation.surface: A seductress is rumoured to have no morals deep down.
explanation.definitionFit: Amoral means lacking any moral sense, having no principles of right and wrong at all.

clue.text: Book some rest here

indicators.note: some means only part of what follows, so the letters lie inside the phrase

parts.note: found within the run of letters across these two words

explanation.surface: Someone suggests reading a book while they relax here.
explanation.definitionFit: Esther is a book of the Old Testament, telling of the Jewish queen of Persia.

clue.text: Seafood glut — one's heading for aitchbone for change?

indicators.note: putting letters up for change invites them to be rearranged into another order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, without the apostrophe

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its opening letter, the one at the front

parts.note: the first letter of aitchbone

explanation.surface: A seafood glut prompts someone to swap to an aitchbone, a cut of beef, for a change.
explanation.definitionFit: A langouste is a spiny lobster, a shellfish eaten as seafood in French cookery.

clue.text: A red?

parts.note: surface reading: a question about a communist
setter's reading: the letter A, coloured red, as in Hawthorne's novel

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'red' as a noun for a leftist and it goes nowhere; the clue describes a capital A in red, the badge of adultery Hester Prynne must wear.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hawthorne's novel the heroine is forced to wear a crimson A sewn on her dress for adultery.

clue.text: Nonsense about sailor's place to sleep

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word's letters go round the other

parts.note: rot means rubbish or nonsense
OS, ordinary seaman, is a common abbreviation for a sailor

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at where a sailor beds down.
explanation.walkthrough: The sailor goes in after the first two letters of the nonsense, not in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A roost is the perch where birds settle for the night, loosely any place to sleep.

clue.text: Old place one's going to — spacious on reflection

parts.note: one is I, and 'is going to' is will, contracted to I'LL

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror shows things back to front, so the word is read the other way

parts.note: an airy room is spacious

explanation.surface: Someone muses on a roomy old place they plan to visit.
explanation.definitionFit: Illyria was an ancient region of the Balkans, the setting of Twelfth Night, so an old place.

clue.text: Take as model one couple limiting sex?

parts.note: Roman numeral one

indicators.note: limiting something means hemming it in on both sides

parts.note: to mate is to couple
IT is old slang for sex appeal, or sex

explanation.surface: A couple restricting their sex life is offered as a role model.
explanation.walkthrough: IT for sex, or sex appeal, comes from an old Kipling usage that crosswords keep alive.
explanation.definitionFit: To imitate someone is to copy them, treating them as an example to follow.

clue.text: I've pals upset with nanny state

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone's friends are upset by government interference, the so-called nanny state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nanny state' reads as one political phrase, but nanny is fodder and state alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pennsylvania is one of the fifty United States, in the American northeast.

clue.text: Woman's daughter needs small drink at first for farm worker

parts.note: s is the abbreviation for small
wine is a drink
her is the possessive for a woman, as in her book
d is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A woman's daughter wants a quick drink before work on the farm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At first' places the small drink before the woman's daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: A swineherd is someone whose job is tending pigs, a traditional farm labourer.

clue.text: Integrate prisoner, European, in flier's part

parts.note: to fuse is to join into one
an old lag is a long-term prisoner
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: Plans to absorb a European prisoner into an aircrew.
explanation.definitionFit: The fuselage is the main body of an aircraft, part of anything that flies.

clue.text: Most heartless site's not flexible

indicators.note: flexible means able to bend into other shapes, so the letters can be reordered

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A cold-hearted planning verdict: this site is not negotiable.
explanation.definitionFit: A stony person is unfeeling, so the superlative describes someone with the least heart of all.

clue.text: Awfully dirty? Bath is useful at outset — in this?

definitions.text: Awfully dirty? Bath is useful at outset — in this?

indicators.note: awfully suggests something done badly, so the letters come out in a mangled order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: the outset of a word is its start, so only its opening letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of useful

explanation.surface: Filthy? A bath is handy to begin with, and you would take it naked.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: when you are filthy and climb into the bath, you wear nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Birthday suit is a jokey idiom for bare skin, as worn at birth, which is how people bathe.

clue.text: Chance holding fool's dog

indicators.note: holding something means having it inside, gripped by the outer word

parts.note: a bet is a gamble, a chance
an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: Someone gambles that the idiot's dog will win.
explanation.definitionFit: A basset is a short-legged hound with long ears, a breed of dog.

clue.text: Exodus — all inside leaving headland in this?

definitions.text: Exodus — all inside leaving headland in this?

indicators.note: if everything inside departs, only the two end letters are left behind

parts.note: the first and last letters of Exodus
a cape is a headland jutting into the sea

explanation.surface: A mass departure, with everyone abandoning a promontory.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as definition: Exodus tells of the Israelites' flight from Egypt.
explanation.definitionFit: An exodus is a mass departure, and an escape is getting away, so everyone leaving is one.

clue.text: Before led by person from Vienna, say, not half serious

indicators.note: not half means only half survives, so the second half of the word is dropped

parts.note: Vienna is the capital of Austria
ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: Someone is introduced by a rather solemn Viennese person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Led by' puts the Viennese piece first; half of AUSTRIAN is AUST.
explanation.definitionFit: Austere describes a stern, grave manner, a close synonym of serious in tone.

clue.text: Japanese, say, ultimately carefree as bird?

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of carefree
taken as written
a tern is a seabird

explanation.surface: A Japanese person is pictured as free as a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free as a bird' is a stock phrase, but bird here gives a specific seabird.
explanation.definitionFit: Japanese is an example of something Eastern, from the Far East of Asia.

clue.text: Opponents at table worry old soldier

parts.note: at the bridge table South and West sit side by side as opponents
to eat someone, as in what's eating you, is to worry them

explanation.surface: Bridge players fret about an elderly veteran.
explanation.walkthrough: Bridge players are known by compass points; North-South and East-West are partners.
explanation.definitionFit: Old sweat is British slang for a veteran soldier, so sweat alone serves as old soldier.

clue.text: Move fast in pursuit of second portion

parts.note: s is the abbreviation for second
to hare is to run very quickly

explanation.surface: Someone dashes off to fetch a second helping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In pursuit of' puts the fast mover after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: A share is one's part or allotment, the same as a portion of something divided.

clue.text: Showing restraint, police force backing exercise charge

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the force's letters run the other way

parts.note: the Met is London's Metropolitan Police
PE, physical education, is school exercise
a rate is a fee or charge

explanation.surface: The police calmly support a fee for fitness classes.
explanation.definitionFit: A temperate person is moderate and self-controlled, which is showing restraint.

clue.text: Article Woodrow oddly ignored about Roosevelt

parts.note: the definite article

indicators.note: ignoring the odd-numbered places leaves the even ones, every other letter

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters of Woodrow
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A newspaper article ignores President Wilson in favour of Roosevelt.
explanation.walkthrough: Woodrow Wilson and Roosevelt were both US presidents, which hides that Woodrow is only letter fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Theodore Roosevelt was the 26th US president, so the first name identifies that Roosevelt.

clue.text: Affirm correctness of a primarily tough examination

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter counts

parts.note: the first letter of tough
a test is an examination

explanation.surface: A hard exam confirms that someone's answers are right.
explanation.definitionFit: To attest something is to bear witness that it is true or genuine.
